case_info.scenario: A 56-year-old woman with a history of multiple myeloma complicated by therapy-related acute myeloid leukemia was admitted for myeloablative conditioning in preparation for allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant. Her course was complicated by severe mucositis, acute kidney injury, and neutropenic fever. During her admission, the patient also developed painful necrotic skin lesions, a nonproductive cough, and altered mental status. Physical examination findings demonstrated dusky, purpuric, and pink papulonodules, some with overlying eschar, scattered on the scalp, neck, trunk, and extremities (Figure, A). Laboratory study results revealed a white blood cell count of 150/μL (reference range, 3500/μL to 10 500/μL), an absolute neutrophil count of 130/μL (reference range, 1500/μL to 7400/μL), and a platelet count of 19 ×103/μL (reference range, 150 ×103/μL to 400 ×103/μL). (To convert the white blood cell and neutrophil counts to cells ×109/L, multiply by 0.001; conversion of the platelet count to cells ×109/L is 1:1.) Blood culture results were negative. The results of a computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain showed no acute intracranial hemorrhage, territorial infarction, or mass effect. The results of a CT scan of the chest demonstrated multifocal bilateral ground-glass patchy opacities, scattered solid bilateral pulmonary nodules, and a moderately sized pericardial effusion. A biopsy specimen from a skin nodule on the left lateral thigh was obtained for histopathologic examination and tissue culture, and wet mount preparation of a tissue culture colony was performed (Figure, B).
case_info.caption: A, Physical examination findings demonstrate dusky and pink papulonodules, some with overlying eschar, scattered on the scalp, neck, and extremities. B, Lactophenol cotton blue staining of a tissue culture colony reveals septated hyphae and oval microconidia.
case_info.explanation: Wet mount preparation of a tissue culture mold colony with lactophenol cotton blue staining revealed septated hyphae and oval microconidia (Figure, B). A fungal culture grewFusarium solani. Fusariumspecies are ubiquitous in soil and air, and transmission occurs through inhalation or direct cutaneous inoculation from a contaminated source.1Localized infections can present as onychomycosis, superficial cutaneous infections, and keratitis in immunocompetent hosts; invasive and disseminated disease is more common in those who are immunocompromised, particularly those with neutropenia.2In those with hematologic cancer, disseminated fusariosis most frequently involves the skin, blood, lungs, and sinuses.3 Although the incidence of fusariosis among patients undergoing hematopoietic transplant is less than 1%, invasive fusariosis has a mortality rate of approximately 80% in individuals with hematologic cancer.4Thus, early recognition is crucial for prompt treatment of the infection. Purpuric patches or papulonodules in this population should be evaluated urgently with skin biopsy and tissue culture. It is also recommended that patients with hematologic cancer who are about to receive chemotherapy and/or bone marrow transplant first undergo a thorough examination for skin findings of onychomycosis, which has been associated withFusariuminfections.1,3,5 The patient’s physical examination findings of scattered and painful purpuric papulonodules are similar to those found in invasive aspergillosis, which has an incidence of 2.7% in patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplant.4Invasive aspergillosis is an infection caused by the fungalAspergillusspecies, which is ubiquitous in the environment.6As transmission is primarily through inhalation, invasive aspergillus most commonly presents with pulmonary or sinus disease that can then progress to dissemination in immunocompromised individuals. BothAspergillusandFusariummay cause elevated serum galactomannan antigen. Chest CT findings of invasive aspergillosis and disseminated fusariosis are similar, and both may show ground-glass opacities, segmental consolidation, cavitary lesions, and the “halo sign” (ground-glass opacities representing hemorrhage surrounding central fungal nodules). Lactophenol cotton blue staining of mold colony can differentiate between the 2 pathogens, asAspergillusspecies have septate hyphae and flask-shaped vesicles.1,7 Ecthyma gangrenosum is a cutaneous infection caused by hematogenous spread of bacteria, most commonlyPseudomonas aeruginosa. It most frequently occurs in immunocompromised individuals, including those with chemotherapy-induced neutropenia.8As this represents bacterial angioinvasion, ecthyma gangrenosum presents as purpuric macules that may become pustular or bullous before progressing to ulcers with overlying eschar most commonly in the anogenital and axillary areas. In most cases,Pseudomonascan be detected from tissue specimens, but blood culture results are often negative.9 Sweet syndrome, also known as acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis, is a rare disorder that is commonly associated with hematologic cancers, such as acute myeloid leukemia. Sweet syndrome can also be associated with other states, such as autoimmune disease, or be due to medications, such as granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. Classic Sweet syndrome presents as tender, erythematous, and edematous plaques associated with fever and leukocytosis. Cutaneous involvement generally does not show overlying eschar, as seen in disseminated fusariosis. Skin biopsy histopathologic features can mimic infection with dermal edema and a dense infiltrate of neutrophils; however, the results of infectious stains and tissue culture will be negative. Systemic corticosteroids are often first-line treatments for Sweet syndrome.10 The patient was treated with intravenous amphotericin B and voriconazole for disseminated fusariosis, with resolution of her cutaneous lesions over the course of 6 weeks. This case highlights the importance of early diagnosis of disseminated fusariosis, especially for those who are immunocompromised or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Wet mount preparation of a tissue culture mold colony with lactophenol cotton blue staining revealed septated hyphae and oval microconidia (Figure, B). A fungal culture grewFusarium solani. Fusariumspecies are ubiquitous in soil and air, and transmission occurs through inhalation or direct cutaneous inoculation from a contaminated source.1Localized infections can present as onychomycosis, superficial cutaneous infections, and keratitis in immunocompetent hosts; invasive and disseminated disease is more common in those who are immunocompromised, particularly those with neutropenia.2In those with hematologic cancer, disseminated fusariosis most frequently involves the skin, blood, lungs, and sinuses.3 Although the incidence of fusariosis among patients undergoing hematopoietic transplant is less than 1%, invasive fusariosis has a mortality rate of approximately 80% in individuals with hematologic cancer.4Thus, early recognition is crucial for prompt treatment of the infection. Purpuric patches or papulonodules in this population should be evaluated urgently with skin biopsy and tissue culture. It is also recommended that patients with hematologic cancer who are about to receive chemotherapy and/or bone marrow transplant first undergo a thorough examination for skin findings of onychomycosis, which has been associated withFusariuminfections.1,3,5 The patient’s physical examination findings of scattered and painful purpuric papulonodules are similar to those found in invasive aspergillosis, which has an incidence of 2.7% in patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplant.4Invasive aspergillosis is an infection caused by the fungalAspergillusspecies, which is ubiquitous in the environment.6As transmission is primarily through inhalation, invasive aspergillus most commonly presents with pulmonary or sinus disease that can then progress to dissemination in immunocompromised individuals. BothAspergillusandFusariummay cause elevated serum galactomannan antigen. Chest CT findings of invasive aspergillosis and disseminated fusariosis are similar, and both may show ground-glass opacities, segmental consolidation, cavitary lesions, and the “halo sign” (ground-glass opacities representing hemorrhage surrounding central fungal nodules). Lactophenol cotton blue staining of mold colony can differentiate between the 2 pathogens, asAspergillusspecies have septate hyphae and flask-shaped vesicles.1,7 Ecthyma gangrenosum is a cutaneous infection caused by hematogenous spread of bacteria, most commonlyPseudomonas aeruginosa. It most frequently occurs in immunocompromised individuals, including those with chemotherapy-induced neutropenia.8As this represents bacterial angioinvasion, ecthyma gangrenosum presents as purpuric macules that may become pustular or bullous before progressing to ulcers with overlying eschar most commonly in the anogenital and axillary areas. In most cases,Pseudomonascan be detected from tissue specimens, but blood culture results are often negative.9 Sweet syndrome, also known as acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis, is a rare disorder that is commonly associated with hematologic cancers, such as acute myeloid leukemia. Sweet syndrome can also be associated with other states, such as autoimmune disease, or be due to medications, such as granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. Classic Sweet syndrome presents as tender, erythematous, and edematous plaques associated with fever and leukocytosis. Cutaneous involvement generally does not show overlying eschar, as seen in disseminated fusariosis. Skin biopsy histopathologic features can mimic infection with dermal edema and a dense infiltrate of neutrophils; however, the results of infectious stains and tissue culture will be negative. Systemic corticosteroids are often first-line treatments for Sweet syndrome.10 The patient was treated with intravenous amphotericin B and voriconazole for disseminated fusariosis, with resolution of her cutaneous lesions over the course of 6 weeks. This case highlights the importance of early diagnosis of disseminated fusariosis, especially for those who are immunocompromised or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]

2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]

Her course was complicated by severe mucositis, acute kidney injury, and neutropenic fever. During her admission, the patient also developed painful necrotic skin lesions, a nonproductive cough, and altered mental status. Physical examination findings demonstrated dusky, purpuric, and pink papulonodules, some with overlying eschar, scattered on the scalp, neck, trunk, and extremities (Figure, A). Laboratory study results revealed a white blood cell count of 150/μL (reference range, 3500/μL to 10 500/μL), an absolute neutrophil count of 130/μL (reference range, 1500/μL to 7400/μL), and a platelet count of 19 ×103/μL (reference range, 150 ×103/μL to 400 ×103/μL). (To convert the white blood cell and neutrophil counts to cells ×109/L, multiply by 0.001; conversion of the platelet count to cells ×109/L is 1:1.) Blood culture results were negative. The results of a computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain showed no acute intracranial hemorrhage, territorial infarction, or mass effect. A biopsy specimen from a skin nodule on the left lateral thigh was obtained for histopathologic examination and tissue culture, and wet mount preparation of a tissue culture colony was performed (Figure, B).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]

{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the

  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 2.2. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

}

case_info.explanation: Wet mount preparation of a tissue culture mold colony with lactophenol cotton blue staining revealed septated hyphae and oval microconidia (Figure, B). A fungal culture grewFusarium solani. Fusariumspecies are ubiquitous in soil and air, and transmission occurs through inhalation or direct cutaneous inoculation from a contaminated source.1Localized infections can present as onychomycosis, superficial cutaneous infections, and keratitis in immunocompetent hosts; invasive and disseminated disease is more common in those who are immunocompromised, particularly those with neutropenia.2In those with hematologic cancer, disseminated fusariosis most frequently involves the skin, blood, lungs, and sinuses.3 Although the incidence of fusariosis among patients undergoing hematopoietic transplant is less than 1%, invasive fusariosis has a mortality rate of approximately 80% in individuals with hematologic cancer.4Thus, early recognition is crucial for prompt treatment of the infection. Purpuric patches or papulonodules in this population should be evaluated urgently with skin biopsy and tissue culture. It is also recommended that patients with hematologic cancer who are about to receive chemotherapy and/or bone marrow transplant first undergo a thorough examination for skin findings of onychomycosis, which has been associated withFusariuminfections.1,3,5 The patient’s physical examination findings of scattered and painful purpuric papulonodules are similar to those found in invasive aspergillosis, which has an incidence of 2.7% in patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplant.4Invasive aspergillosis is an infection caused by the fungalAspergillusspecies, which is ubiquitous in the environment.6As transmission is primarily through inhalation, invasive aspergillus most commonly presents with pulmonary or sinus disease that can then progress to dissemination in immunocompromised individuals. BothAspergillusandFusariummay cause elevated serum galactomannan antigen. Chest CT findings of invasive aspergillosis and disseminated fusariosis are similar, and both may show ground-glass opacities, segmental consolidation, cavitary lesions, and the “halo sign” (ground-glass opacities representing hemorrhage surrounding central fungal nodules). Lactophenol cotton blue staining of mold colony can differentiate between the 2 pathogens, asAspergillusspecies have septate hyphae and flask-shaped vesicles.1,7 Ecthyma gangrenosum is a cutaneous infection caused by hematogenous spread of bacteria, most commonlyPseudomonas aeruginosa. It most frequently occurs in immunocompromised individuals, including those with chemotherapy-induced neutropenia.8As this represents bacterial angioinvasion, ecthyma gangrenosum presents as purpuric macules that may become pustular or bullous before progressing to ulcers with overlying eschar most commonly in the anogenital and axillary areas. In most cases,Pseudomonascan be detected from tissue specimens, but blood culture results are often negative.9 Sweet syndrome, also known as acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis, is a rare disorder that is commonly associated with hematologic cancers, such as acute myeloid leukemia. Sweet syndrome can also be associated with other states, such as autoimmune disease, or be due to medications, such as granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. Classic Sweet syndrome presents as tender, erythematous, and edematous plaques associated with fever and leukocytosis. Cutaneous involvement generally does not show overlying eschar, as seen in disseminated fusariosis. Skin biopsy histopathologic features can mimic infection with dermal edema and a dense infiltrate of neutrophils; however, the results of infectious stains and tissue culture will be negative. Systemic corticosteroids are often first-line treatments for Sweet syndrome.10 The patient was treated with intravenous amphotericin B and voriconazole for disseminated fusariosis, with resolution of her cutaneous lesions over the course of 6 weeks. This case highlights the importance of early diagnosis of disseminated fusariosis, especially for those who are immunocompromised or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy.

case_info.explanation: Wet mount preparation of a tissue culture mold colony with lactophenol cotton blue staining revealed septated hyphae and oval microconidia (Figure, B). A fungal culture grewFusarium solani. Fusariumspecies are ubiquitous in soil and air, and transmission occurs through inhalation or direct cutaneous inoculation from a contaminated source.1Localized infections can present as onychomycosis, superficial cutaneous infections, and keratitis in immunocompetent hosts; invasive and disseminated disease is more common in those who are immunocompromised, particularly those with neutropenia.2In those with hematologic cancer, disseminated fusariosis most frequently involves the skin, blood, lungs, and sinuses.3 Although the incidence of fusariosis among patients undergoing hematopoietic transplant is less than 1%, invasive fusariosis has a mortality rate of approximately 80% in individuals with hematologic cancer.4Thus, early recognition is crucial for prompt treatment of the infection. Purpuric patches or papulonodules in this population should be evaluated urgently with skin biopsy and tissue culture. It is also recommended that patients with hematologic cancer who are about to receive chemotherapy and/or bone marrow transplant first undergo a thorough examination for skin findings of onychomycosis, which has been associated withFusariuminfections.1,3,5 The patient’s physical examination findings of scattered and painful purpuric papulonodules are similar to those found in invasive aspergillosis, which has an incidence of 2.7% in patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplant.4Invasive aspergillosis is an infection caused by the fungalAspergillusspecies, which is ubiquitous in the environment.6As transmission is primarily through inhalation, invasive aspergillus most commonly presents with pulmonary or sinus disease that can then progress to dissemination in immunocompromised individuals. BothAspergillusandFusariummay cause elevated serum galactomannan antigen. Chest CT findings of invasive aspergillosis and disseminated fusariosis are similar, and both may show ground-glass opacities, segmental consolidation, cavitary lesions, and the “halo sign” (ground-glass opacities representing hemorrhage surrounding central fungal nodules). Lactophenol cotton blue staining of mold colony can differentiate between the 2 pathogens, asAspergillusspecies have septate hyphae and flask-shaped vesicles.1,7 Ecthyma gangrenosum is a cutaneous infection caused by hematogenous spread of bacteria, most commonlyPseudomonas aeruginosa. It most frequently occurs in immunocompromised individuals, including those with chemotherapy-induced neutropenia.8As this represents bacterial angioinvasion, ecthyma gangrenosum presents as purpuric macules that may become pustular or bullous before progressing to ulcers with overlying eschar most commonly in the anogenital and axillary areas. In most cases,Pseudomonascan be detected from tissue specimens, but blood culture results are often negative.9 Sweet syndrome, also known as acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis, is a rare disorder that is commonly associated with hematologic cancers, such as acute myeloid leukemia. Sweet syndrome can also be associated with other states, such as autoimmune disease, or be due to medications, such as granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. Classic Sweet syndrome presents as tender, erythematous, and edematous plaques associated with fever and leukocytosis. Cutaneous involvement generally does not show overlying eschar, as seen in disseminated fusariosis. Skin biopsy histopathologic features can mimic infection with dermal edema and a dense infiltrate of neutrophils; however, the results of infectious stains and tissue culture will be negative. Systemic corticosteroids are often first-line treatments for Sweet syndrome.10 The patient was treated with intravenous amphotericin B and voriconazole for disseminated fusariosis, with resolution of her cutaneous lesions over the course of 6 weeks. This case highlights the importance of early diagnosis of disseminated fusariosis, especially for those who are immunocompromised or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 56-year-old woman with a history of multiple myeloma complicated by therapy-related acute myeloid leukemia was admitted for myeloablative conditioning in preparation for allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant. Her course was complicated by severe mucositis, acute kidney injury, and neutropenic fever. During her admission, the patient also developed painful necrotic skin lesions, a nonproductive cough, and altered mental status. Physical examination findings demonstrated dusky, purpuric, and pink papulonodules, some with overlying eschar, scattered on the scalp, neck, trunk, and extremities (Figure, A). Laboratory study results revealed a white blood cell count of 150/μL (reference range, 3500/μL to 10 500/μL), an absolute neutrophil count of 130/μL (reference range, 1500/μL to 7400/μL), and a platelet count of 19 ×103/μL (reference range, 150 ×103/μL to 400 ×103/μL). (To convert the white blood cell and neutrophil counts to cells ×109/L, multiply by 0.001; conversion of the platelet count to cells ×109/L is 1:1.) Blood culture results were negative. The results of a computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain showed no acute intracranial hemorrhage, territorial infarction, or mass effect. The results of a CT scan of the chest demonstrated multifocal bilateral ground-glass patchy opacities, scattered solid bilateral pulmonary nodules, and a moderately sized pericardial effusion. A biopsy specimen from a skin nodule on the left lateral thigh was obtained for histopathologic examination and tissue culture, and wet mount preparation of a tissue culture colony was performed (Figure, B).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

The most appropriate next step in management for this patient is A. Disseminated fusariosis. Given her immunocompromised status due to multiple myeloma and acute myeloid leukemia, combined with the findings of skin lesions, respiratory symptoms, and the presence of septated hyphae in the tissue culture, fusariosis is highly suggestive and a significant concern in this scenario.

I agree that disseminated fusariosis is a strong consideration given the presentation, but we should also consider other angioinvasive molds like Aspergillus or Mucorales, which can have similar histopathology. The key next step is to initiate broad-spectrum antifungal therapy immediately, such as voriconazole or liposomal amphotericin B, while awaiting species identification from the tissue culture.

While I acknowledge the importance of considering other molds, the histopathology showing septated hyphae is particularly indicative of fusariosis in this patient’s context. Immediate initiation of antifungal therapy targeting fusariosis is crucial. We can administer liposomal amphotericin B, which is effective for both fusariosis and other molds, while we await further culture identification.

That's a sound plan. Liposomal amphotericin B is an excellent empiric choice given its coverage for Fusarium and other angioinvasive molds like Aspergillus. We should also continue supportive care for her neutropenia and consider surgical consultation for debridement of necrotic skin lesions if feasible.

I appreciate your acknowledgment of the need for broad-spectrum antifungal therapy. However, given the clear indication of fusariosis from the histopathology showing septated hyphae, I believe our priority should be to initiate therapy specifically targeting this condition. Liposomal amphotericin B is an appropriate choice. Supportive care and potential surgical intervention for the necrotic lesions are also vital components of her management.

Agreed. Starting liposomal amphotericin B provides necessary coverage while we finalize the diagnosis. We should also ensure the microbiology lab is performing fungal speciation and antifungal susceptibility testing on the tissue isolate to guide potential future therapy adjustments.

[Clinician's current statement]
Your points about initiating broad-spectrum antifungal therapy and microbiological testing are well taken. However, the definitive histopathological evidence of septated hyphae strongly supports fusariosis as the primary concern, making it essential to start therapy specifically targeting this condition. Liposomal amphotericin B remains the most appropriate choice at this time, along with supportive measures.

Respond directly to this statement.

Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the

mistake -- keep them separate:

[Important rules]

* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is

  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

(To convert the white blood cell and neutrophil counts to cells ×109/L, multiply by 0.001; conversion of the platelet count to cells ×109/L is 1:1.) Blood culture results were negative. case_info.caption: A, Physical examination findings demonstrate dusky and pink papulonodules, some with overlying eschar, scattered on the scalp, neck, and extremities. B, Lactophenol cotton blue staining of a tissue culture colony reveals septated hyphae and oval microconidia.
case_info.explanation: Wet mount preparation of a tissue culture mold colony with lactophenol cotton blue staining revealed septated hyphae and oval microconidia (Figure, B). A fungal culture grewFusarium solani. Fusariumspecies are ubiquitous in soil and air, and transmission occurs through inhalation or direct cutaneous inoculation from a contaminated source.1Localized infections can present as onychomycosis, superficial cutaneous infections, and keratitis in immunocompetent hosts; invasive and disseminated disease is more common in those who are immunocompromised, particularly those with neutropenia.2In those with hematologic cancer, disseminated fusariosis most frequently involves the skin, blood, lungs, and sinuses.3 Although the incidence of fusariosis among patients undergoing hematopoietic transplant is less than 1%, invasive fusariosis has a mortality rate of approximately 80% in individuals with hematologic cancer.4Thus, early recognition is crucial for prompt treatment of the infection. Purpuric patches or papulonodules in this population should be evaluated urgently with skin biopsy and tissue culture. It is also recommended that patients with hematologic cancer who are about to receive chemotherapy and/or bone marrow transplant first undergo a thorough examination for skin findings of onychomycosis, which has been associated withFusariuminfections.1,3,5 The patient’s physical examination findings of scattered and painful purpuric papulonodules are similar to those found in invasive aspergillosis, which has an incidence of 2.7% in patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplant.4Invasive aspergillosis is an infection caused by the fungalAspergillusspecies, which is ubiquitous in the environment.6As transmission is primarily through inhalation, invasive aspergillus most commonly presents with pulmonary or sinus disease that can then progress to dissemination in immunocompromised individuals. BothAspergillusandFusariummay cause elevated serum galactomannan antigen. Chest CT findings of invasive aspergillosis and disseminated fusariosis are similar, and both may show ground-glass opacities, segmental consolidation, cavitary lesions, and the “halo sign” (ground-glass opacities representing hemorrhage surrounding central fungal nodules). Lactophenol cotton blue staining of mold colony can differentiate between the 2 pathogens, asAspergillusspecies have septate hyphae and flask-shaped vesicles.1,7 Ecthyma gangrenosum is a cutaneous infection caused by hematogenous spread of bacteria, most commonlyPseudomonas aeruginosa. It most frequently occurs in immunocompromised individuals, including those with chemotherapy-induced neutropenia.8As this represents bacterial angioinvasion, ecthyma gangrenosum presents as purpuric macules that may become pustular or bullous before progressing to ulcers with overlying eschar most commonly in the anogenital and axillary areas. In most cases,Pseudomonascan be detected from tissue specimens, but blood culture results are often negative.9 Sweet syndrome, also known as acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis, is a rare disorder that is commonly associated with hematologic cancers, such as acute myeloid leukemia. Sweet syndrome can also be associated with other states, such as autoimmune disease, or be due to medications, such as granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. Classic Sweet syndrome presents as tender, erythematous, and edematous plaques associated with fever and leukocytosis. Cutaneous involvement generally does not show overlying eschar, as seen in disseminated fusariosis. Skin biopsy histopathologic features can mimic infection with dermal edema and a dense infiltrate of neutrophils; however, the results of infectious stains and tissue culture will be negative. Systemic corticosteroids are often first-line treatments for Sweet syndrome.10 The patient was treated with intravenous amphotericin B and voriconazole for disseminated fusariosis, with resolution of her cutaneous lesions over the course of 6 weeks. This case highlights the importance of early diagnosis of disseminated fusariosis, especially for those who are immunocompromised or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy.

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"

* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

case_info.explanation: Wet mount preparation of a tissue culture mold colony with lactophenol cotton blue staining revealed septated hyphae and oval microconidia (Figure, B). A fungal culture grewFusarium solani. Fusariumspecies are ubiquitous in soil and air, and transmission occurs through inhalation or direct cutaneous inoculation from a contaminated source.1Localized infections can present as onychomycosis, superficial cutaneous infections, and keratitis in immunocompetent hosts; invasive and disseminated disease is more common in those who are immunocompromised, particularly those with neutropenia.2In those with hematologic cancer, disseminated fusariosis most frequently involves the skin, blood, lungs, and sinuses.3 Although the incidence of fusariosis among patients undergoing hematopoietic transplant is less than 1%, invasive fusariosis has a mortality rate of approximately 80% in individuals with hematologic cancer.4Thus, early recognition is crucial for prompt treatment of the infection. Purpuric patches or papulonodules in this population should be evaluated urgently with skin biopsy and tissue culture. It is also recommended that patients with hematologic cancer who are about to receive chemotherapy and/or bone marrow transplant first undergo a thorough examination for skin findings of onychomycosis, which has been associated withFusariuminfections.1,3,5 The patient’s physical examination findings of scattered and painful purpuric papulonodules are similar to those found in invasive aspergillosis, which has an incidence of 2.7% in patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplant.4Invasive aspergillosis is an infection caused by the fungalAspergillusspecies, which is ubiquitous in the environment.6As transmission is primarily through inhalation, invasive aspergillus most commonly presents with pulmonary or sinus disease that can then progress to dissemination in immunocompromised individuals. BothAspergillusandFusariummay cause elevated serum galactomannan antigen. Chest CT findings of invasive aspergillosis and disseminated fusariosis are similar, and both may show ground-glass opacities, segmental consolidation, cavitary lesions, and the “halo sign” (ground-glass opacities representing hemorrhage surrounding central fungal nodules). Lactophenol cotton blue staining of mold colony can differentiate between the 2 pathogens, asAspergillusspecies have septate hyphae and flask-shaped vesicles.1,7 Ecthyma gangrenosum is a cutaneous infection caused by hematogenous spread of bacteria, most commonlyPseudomonas aeruginosa. It most frequently occurs in immunocompromised individuals, including those with chemotherapy-induced neutropenia.8As this represents bacterial angioinvasion, ecthyma gangrenosum presents as purpuric macules that may become pustular or bullous before progressing to ulcers with overlying eschar most commonly in the anogenital and axillary areas. In most cases,Pseudomonascan be detected from tissue specimens, but blood culture results are often negative.9 Sweet syndrome, also known as acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis, is a rare disorder that is commonly associated with hematologic cancers, such as acute myeloid leukemia. Sweet syndrome can also be associated with other states, such as autoimmune disease, or be due to medications, such as granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. Classic Sweet syndrome presents as tender, erythematous, and edematous plaques associated with fever and leukocytosis. Cutaneous involvement generally does not show overlying eschar, as seen in disseminated fusariosis. Skin biopsy histopathologic features can mimic infection with dermal edema and a dense infiltrate of neutrophils; however, the results of infectious stains and tissue culture will be negative. Systemic corticosteroids are often first-line treatments for Sweet syndrome.10 The patient was treated with intravenous amphotericin B and voriconazole for disseminated fusariosis, with resolution of her cutaneous lesions over the course of 6 weeks. This case highlights the importance of early diagnosis of disseminated fusariosis, especially for those who are immunocompromised or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy.

[Case]
A 56-year-old woman with a history of multiple myeloma complicated by therapy-related acute myeloid leukemia was admitted for myeloablative conditioning in preparation for allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant. The results of a CT scan of the chest demonstrated multifocal bilateral ground-glass patchy opacities, scattered solid bilateral pulmonary nodules, and a moderately sized pericardial effusion. A biopsy specimen from a skin nodule on the left lateral thigh was obtained for histopathologic examination and tissue culture, and wet mount preparation of a tissue culture colony was performed (Figure, B).
